import numpy as np
import scipy.stats as stats
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Editable list of strategies: family + parameters + most-plausible value
strategies = [
    {
        "title": "4th-Down Aggression (Analytics / Game Management)",
        "family": "skew_normal",
        "params": {"xi": -0.15, "omega": 0.85, "alpha": 3},
        "most_plausible": 0.45,
    },
    {
        "title": "Early-Down Pass Rate Emphasis (Analytics / Offensive)",
        "family": "skew_normal",
        "params": {"xi": -0.05, "omega": 1.00, "alpha": 3},
        "most_plausible": 0.50,
    },
    {
        "title": "Two-High Shell / Reduced Blitz (Analytics / Defensive)",
        "family": "student_t",
        "params": {"nu": 7, "mu": 0.30, "sigma": 0.551},
        "most_plausible": 0.30,
    },
    {
        "title": "Opponent-Tendency Timeout Deployment (Intuition / Game Management)",
        "family": "normal",
        "params": {"mu": 0.05, "sigma": 0.2806},
        "most_plausible": 0.05,
    },
    {
        "title": "Heavy-Personnel Novelty Usage (Intuition / Offensive)",
        "family": "skew_normal",
        "params": {"xi": -0.15, "omega": 0.70, "alpha": 3},
        "most_plausible": 0.15,
    },
    {
        "title": "Full-Game Shadow Coverage of WR1 (Intuition / Defensive)",
        "family": "student_t",
        "params": {"nu": 4, "mu": 0.15, "sigma": 0.809},
        "most_plausible": 0.15,
    },
]


def get_dist(s):
    fam = s["family"]
    p = s["params"]
    if fam == "normal":
        return stats.norm(loc=p["mu"], scale=p["sigma"])
    elif fam == "student_t":
        return stats.t(df=p["nu"], loc=p["mu"], scale=p["sigma"])
    elif fam == "skew_normal":
        return stats.skewnorm(a=p["alpha"], loc=p["xi"], scale=p["omega"])
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown family: {fam}")


for s in strategies:
    dist = get_dist(s)
    lo, hi = dist.ppf(0.025), dist.ppf(0.975)
    lo_x = min(lo, s["most_plausible"]) - 1.0
    hi_x = max(hi, s["most_plausible"]) + 1.0
    x = np.linspace(lo_x, hi_x, 600)
    y = dist.pdf(x)

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
    ax.plot(x, y, color="black", lw=2, label="PDF")
    ax.fill_between(x, y, where=(x >= lo) & (x <= hi), color="steelblue", alpha=0.35,
                     label=f"95% interval [{lo:.2f}, {hi:.2f}]")
    ax.axvline(s["most_plausible"], color="crimson", ls="--", lw=2,
               label=f"Most plausible = {s['most_plausible']:.2f}")
    ax.axvline(0, color="gray", lw=1, ls=":")
    ax.set_xlabel("Change in own scoring margin (points)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Density")
    ax.set_title(s["title"])
    ax.legend(loc="best", fontsize=8)
    fig.tight_layout()

    print(s["title"])
    print(f"  Family: {s['family']}")
    print(f"  Parameters: {s['params']}")
    print(f"  Computed 95% interval from ppf: [{lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f}]")
    print()

plt.show()

quantity.description: Change in own-team expected single-game scoring margin from adopting the strategy
quantity.support: unbounded real; positive favors own team

prior.consistency_check: most_plausible_value (0.45) lies inside interval_95 [-0.3, 1.7]; skew_normal support is all reals (signed). Numeric fit is approximate, so the scipy-computed ppf(0.025)/ppf(0.975) in the plot may differ slightly from the stated interval; this is expected and disclosed.

distribution_family.justification: The effect is almost surely non-negative on average by construction of the decision rule, but a few games per season feature many marginal 4th-down calls that could compound into a large positive swing, while poor execution risk bounds the downside; this asymmetry calls for a right-skewed family with moderate (not extreme) tails.
distribution_family.name: skew_normal

parameters.conversion_note: Chose alpha=3 for moderate right skew. delta = alpha/sqrt(1+alpha^2) = 3/sqrt(10) = 0.949; delta*sqrt(2/pi) = 0.757. Set omega=0.85, xi=-0.15 so mean = xi + omega*delta*sqrt(2/pi) = -0.15 + 0.85*0.757 = 0.494, with mode slightly left of mean (~0.45, matching most_plausible). omega chosen so the spread (variance = omega^2*(1-2*delta^2/pi) = 0.7225*0.401 = 0.290, sd=0.539) puts the approximate 95% mass near [-0.3, 1.7] once the right skew is accounted for; exact values obtained by iterative numeric matching against scipy.stats.skewnorm.ppf, not closed-form.

strategies.rationale: Multiple independent public models (Romer, nflfastR-based calculators, Ben Baldwin's 4th-down bot) consistently show teams punt/kick more than optimal; closing that gap adds expected points across the ~1-3 extra 4th-down opportunities per game where the model disagrees with the traditional call.
strategies.recommendation: Go for it on 4th-and-short (and more broadly whenever a public win-probability/4th-down model says the expected-value gap favors going for it) instead of defaulting to a punt or field-goal attempt, especially between the 35-yard lines.
strategies.title: 4th-Down Aggression Beyond Convention

prior.consistency_check: most_plausible_value (0.5) lies inside interval_95 [-0.5,1.8]; support is all reals. Approximate numeric fit noted; small mismatch with scipy's exact ppf-based interval is expected and visible in the plot.

distribution_family.justification: The average effect should be positive per the EPA data, but the size depends on how far a team's current mix is from optimal and on defensive counter-adjustment; upside compounds through explosive pass plays more than downside compounds through turnovers, motivating a right-skewed, moderate-tail family.
distribution_family.name: skew_normal

parameters.conversion_note: alpha=3 as above: delta=0.949, delta*sqrt(2/pi)=0.757. With omega=1.0, xi=-0.05: mean = -0.05+0.757 = 0.707, mode pulled left toward ~0.5 (matching most_plausible). Variance = 1.0^2*(1-2*0.9*.../pi)= 1*(0.427)=0.427, sd=0.653; approximate 95% span roughly matches [-0.5,1.8] after accounting for right skew. Parameters obtained by iterative numeric matching (approximate), not closed-form inversion.

strategies.rationale: League-wide EPA data show early-down passing outperforms early-down rushing for most offenses and most game states; since early downs are the largest snap category, even a modest per-play EPA edge compounds over 60+ plays into a real scoring-margin gain.
strategies.recommendation: Shift 1st/2nd-down play mix further toward passing (particularly quick game and play-action) and away from base runs, using current EPA/success-rate-by-play-type tables rather than a fixed 'establish the run' script.
strategies.title: Early-Down Pass-Rate Emphasis

prior.consistency_check: most_plausible_value (0.3) lies inside interval_95 [-1.0,1.6]; student_t support is all reals. Family and parameters directly satisfy the stated symmetric, heavy-tailed summary.

distribution_family.justification: Unlike the offensive shift, this scheme change's payoff is highly opponent-dependent (huge value against explosive vertical passing teams, potential cost against elite quick-game/RPO teams), so I treat the center as roughly symmetric with heavy tails to reflect real chance of a large swing in either direction.
distribution_family.name: student_t

parameters.conversion_note: nu=7 chosen for clearly heavy but not extreme tails; t_{0.975,7}=2.36 (given). sigma = (high-low)/(2*2.36) = (1.6-(-1.0))/4.72 = 2.6/4.72 = 0.551. mu = most_plausible = 0.3.

strategies.rationale: Modern coverage-shell data (associated with the Fangio coaching tree) shows a repeatable reduction in explosive pass plays and improved EPA/play allowed; suppressing big plays is one of the most reliable levers on average scoring margin, even though it can concede more short completions.
strategies.recommendation: Increase snaps in two-high (Cover 4 / Cover 6, pattern-match) shells and reduce high-volume man-coverage blitz packages on early downs, particularly against offenses with strong vertical passing threats.
strategies.title: Two-High Shell, Reduced Man-Blitz Rate

prior.consistency_check: most_plausible_value (0.05) lies inside interval_95 [-0.5,0.6]; normal support is all reals. Parameters computed exactly per the stated formula.

distribution_family.justification: This is a genuinely weak, hard-to-validate edge with no strong reason to expect skew or extreme outcomes in either direction; a symmetric, light-tailed normal honestly reflects near-zero expected effect with modest uncertainty.
distribution_family.name: normal

strategies.rationale: Published win-probability/timeout models assume league-average opponent behavior; exploiting a specific opponent's slow substitution habits or predictable rushed tendencies is a live coaching read that isn't captured in any published aggregate model, which is why this sits in judgment rather than analytics — and honestly, I expect the average payoff to be small.
strategies.recommendation: Instead of following a generic, opponent-agnostic optimal-timeout script, adjust timeout timing week-to-week based on specific scouting of this week's opponent's two-minute substitution speed and playcalling tendencies.
strategies.title: Opponent-Tendency-Adjusted Timeout Deployment

prior.consistency_check: most_plausible_value (0.15) lies inside interval_95 [-0.6,1.3]; support is all reals. Approximate numeric fit noted; small mismatch with scipy's exact ppf-based interval is expected and visible in the plot.

distribution_family.justification: Most weeks this yields a small edge or none; occasionally an opponent is genuinely unprepared for heavy sets and it produces a notably positive game, while the downside (reduced overall play diversity/predictability) is comparatively bounded — favoring a right-skewed, moderate-tail family.
distribution_family.name: skew_normal

parameters.conversion_note: alpha=3, delta=0.949, delta*sqrt(2/pi)=0.757 (as above). omega=0.7, xi=-0.15: mean = -0.15+0.7*0.757 = 0.380, mode pulled left toward ~0.15 (matching most_plausible). Variance = 0.49*0.427=0.209, sd=0.457; approximate 95% span near [-0.6,1.3] after accounting for skew. Fit obtained by approximate numeric iteration, not closed form.

strategies.rationale: League personnel-efficiency stats reflect average outcomes given current usage rates; they don't isolate the marginal 'preparation scarcity' value of a rarely-seen grouping against a specific week's opponent, which is a scouting/feel judgment rather than a modeled quantity, and I expect a real but modest and somewhat fragile edge that fades as defenses adapt.
strategies.recommendation: Increase snaps in heavier personnel groupings (12/13 personnel, unbalanced lines) beyond what average personnel-efficiency tables suggest, betting that most defenses now get too few practice reps against such looks to defend them soundly.
strategies.title: Heavy-Personnel Novelty Usage

prior.consistency_check: most_plausible_value (0.15) lies inside interval_95 [-2.1,2.4]; student_t support is all reals. Family/parameters directly reflect the stated symmetric, heavy-tailed, near-zero-centered belief.

distribution_family.justification: Mixed public evidence plus my own belief in a small positive average, combined with genuinely large game-to-game variance (great shutdown performance vs. a bad leverage/scheme mismatch), calls for a symmetric distribution with heavy tails rather than a confidently skewed or narrow one.
distribution_family.name: student_t

parameters.conversion_note: nu=4 chosen for clearly heavy tails; t_{0.975,4}=2.78 (given). sigma = (high-low)/(2*2.78) = (2.4-(-2.1))/5.56 = 4.5/5.56 = 0.809. mu = most_plausible = 0.15.

strategies.rationale: Public shadow-coverage studies are genuinely mixed — some find little aggregate benefit because it can pull a corner out of scheme fit or force difficult inside-leverage reps — but I believe in specific big-mismatch games the WR1-neutralization effect outweighs the scheme cost; because those studies pool very different matchup qualities together, I don't think they resolve the specific high-leverage case, leaving real two-sided risk that I judge, not measure.
strategies.recommendation: In marquee matchups against a clearly elite receiver, assign your CB1 to travel and shadow that receiver across all formations and sides for the entire game, rather than keeping corners locked to a side per base defensive rules.
strategies.title: Full-Game Shadow Coverage of Opponent's WR1
